Goose Creek, South Carolina has grown from a quiet military suburb into one of the fastest-expanding cities in the Charleston metro area, and its roads have not kept pace with the population surge. Tens of thousands of commuters, military personnel from Joint Base Charleston, and commercial trucks share corridors like US-52 every day, creating conditions that produce serious and fatal crashes at alarming rates. If you have been injured in a car accident in Goose Creek or the surrounding Berkeley County area, understanding your legal rights is the first step toward recovering the compensation you need.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Goose Creek's population has grown by more than 30 percent since 2010, making it one of the largest cities in the Lowcountry. That population boom has brought new residential developments, commercial centers, and thousands of additional vehicles onto a road network that was originally designed for a fraction of current traffic volumes. The result is a growing number of intersection collisions, rear-end crashes, and high-speed wrecks that overwhelm local emergency services and leave victims with life-altering injuries.

Goose Creek's Rapid Growth and Rising Traffic Dangers

Goose Creek sits at the intersection of rapid suburban development and heavy military and industrial traffic. New neighborhoods continue to spring up along corridors like US-176 and Henry E. Brown Jr. Boulevard, feeding more vehicles onto roads that already struggle with congestion during peak hours. Shopping centers along St. James Avenue and Red Bank Road generate turning conflicts and pedestrian hazards that did not exist a decade ago.

The city's geography compounds the problem. Goose Creek is bordered by the Naval Weapons Station to the south and west, which limits the number of through-routes available to drivers. Instead of a grid that distributes traffic across multiple roads, most commuters are funneled onto a handful of arterial corridors, concentrating volume and increasing the likelihood of multi-vehicle crashes during rush hour. Drivers heading toward North Charleston, Hanahan, or Ladson often share these same bottleneck routes, amplifying congestion during morning and afternoon commutes.

Infrastructure improvements have lagged well behind development. Road-widening projects, new traffic signals, and intersection redesigns are underway in some areas, but construction zones themselves create temporary hazards — lane shifts, reduced speed zones, and confused traffic patterns that lead to crashes. Residents who drive these roads daily know the danger zones, but unfamiliar drivers, delivery vehicles, and military personnel rotating into the area encounter them with no warning.

Military Traffic From Joint Base Charleston

Joint Base Charleston's Naval Weapons Station occupies a massive footprint adjacent to Goose Creek, and the base is one of the region's largest employers. Approximately 23,000 military and civilian personnel report to the joint base daily, and a significant portion of that workforce lives in Goose Creek neighborhoods that offer affordable housing within minutes of the base gates.

The impact on Goose Creek's roads is substantial. During morning and evening shift changes, traffic queues at base gates back up onto public roads, creating lines of stopped vehicles on routes where other drivers are traveling at full speed. Redbank Road and the secondary access roads connecting Goose Creek to the Naval Weapons Station were not engineered for this volume. Drivers approaching gate queues may not see stopped traffic until it is too late, particularly during early morning shifts when visibility is low.

Military convoys and oversized equipment transports also use Goose Creek's public roads. These vehicles are slower, wider, and harder to maneuver than standard passenger cars, and they create passing hazards on two-lane roads. When impatient civilian drivers attempt to pass military vehicles in no-passing zones, the consequences can be catastrophic. The mix of military and civilian traffic patterns is a defining feature of driving in Goose Creek, and it contributes to accident types that are uncommon in other suburban communities.

The US-52 Corridor: Berkeley County's Most Dangerous Road

US-52 — known locally as Goose Creek Boulevard within the city and Rivers Avenue as it continues into North Charleston — is the spine of Berkeley County's traffic network and one of the most dangerous corridors in the entire Lowcountry. The road connects Goose Creek to North Charleston, Interstate 26, and the Charleston port facilities, carrying a mix of commuter traffic, commercial trucks, and military vehicles at speeds that frequently exceed the posted limits.

Several characteristics make US-52 particularly hazardous through the Goose Creek and Berkeley County stretch:

  • High speed with frequent access points — The road carries traffic at 45 to 55 miles per hour through areas with numerous driveways, shopping center entrances, and side street intersections, creating constant speed differentials between through traffic and turning vehicles
  • Heavy truck volumes — Commercial trucks serving the port, construction sites, and industrial operations share the road with passenger vehicles, and the size and stopping distance of these vehicles make collisions more severe
  • Inadequate turn lanes — Many intersections along US-52 lack dedicated turn lanes, forcing left-turning vehicles to stop in the travel lane while through traffic approaches at speed from behind
  • Poor lighting — Stretches of US-52 between Goose Creek and North Charleston are poorly lit, contributing to nighttime crashes involving pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles making unexpected turns

Rear-end collisions, T-bone crashes at intersections, and sideswipe accidents during lane changes are the most common crash types along US-52. When a fully loaded commercial truck is involved, the injuries are often catastrophic or fatal.

Common Crash Types in Goose Creek

The combination of military traffic, suburban growth, and high-speed arterials produces a predictable pattern of car accidents throughout the Goose Creek area:

  • Rear-end collisions — The most frequent crash type, caused by sudden stops in congested traffic, gate queues near the Naval Weapons Station, and distracted driving on US-52
  • Intersection T-bone crashes — Red-light running and failure to yield at intersections along St. James Avenue, Henry E. Brown Jr. Boulevard, and US-176 produce broadside collisions that strike vehicles in the most vulnerable areas
  • Head-on collisions — Impaired driving, drowsy driving, and illegal passing on two-lane roads near the base create head-on crash risks, especially during early morning and late-night hours
  • Multi-vehicle pileups — Chain-reaction crashes on US-52 during rush hour, often triggered by a single rear-end collision that cascades through stopped or slow-moving traffic
  • Commercial truck crashes — Trucks entering and exiting industrial sites and port-bound corridors collide with passenger vehicles at intersections and merge points along US-52 and I-26
  • Construction zone accidents — Ongoing road improvement projects create lane shifts, reduced speeds, and confused traffic patterns that increase the risk of sideswipe and rear-end crashes

Serious Injuries in Goose Creek Accidents

The high speeds on US-52, the presence of heavy military and commercial vehicles, and the volume of traffic on Goose Creek's arterials mean that crashes in this area frequently produce severe injuries:

  • Traumatic brain injuries — High-speed collisions and T-bone crashes can cause traumatic brain injuries ranging from concussions with lingering post-concussion syndrome to severe TBI requiring lifetime care and resulting in permanent cognitive deficits
  • Spinal cord injuries — Rear-end collisions and rollover crashes cause herniated discs, spinal fractures, and in the worst cases, partial or complete paralysis
  • Broken bones and crush injuries — Broadside impacts and collisions with commercial trucks can crush vehicle compartments, causing complex fractures that require multiple surgeries and extended rehabilitation
  • Internal organ damage — The force of high-speed collisions can cause internal bleeding, organ lacerations, and abdominal injuries that may not be immediately apparent but are life-threatening without emergency treatment
  • Wrongful death — Head-on collisions, truck underride crashes, and high-speed intersection accidents on Goose Creek's major corridors produce fatal injuries that leave families devastated and facing sudden financial hardship

Many of these injuries require emergency helicopter transport to MUSC or Trident Medical Center, followed by weeks or months of hospitalization, multiple surgeries, and long-term rehabilitation. The medical costs alone can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars before the victim even begins outpatient recovery.

Who Is Liable in a Goose Creek Car Accident?

Determining liability in a Goose Creek car accident depends on the specific circumstances of the crash. Potentially liable parties include:

  • At-fault drivers — Drivers who were speeding, distracted, impaired, or otherwise negligent bear primary responsibility for the crashes they cause
  • Trucking companies — When a commercial truck driver causes a crash, the trucking company may be liable under respondeat superior for the driver's negligence, and may face additional claims for negligent hiring, inadequate training, or hours-of-service violations
  • The federal government — If a military vehicle or federal employee acting within the scope of duty caused the accident, civilians may file a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act
  • Government entities responsible for road maintenance — Berkeley County and SCDOT may be liable if dangerous road conditions, missing signage, malfunctioning traffic signals, or inadequate construction zone markings contributed to the crash
  • Vehicle and parts manufacturers — Defective brakes, tires, airbags, or other components that contributed to the crash or worsened injuries can give rise to product liability claims

In many Goose Creek accidents, more than one party shares fault. An experienced attorney will investigate all potential defendants to maximize your recovery.

Berkeley County Jurisdiction and Local Courts

Goose Creek is located in Berkeley County, South Carolina, which means that most car accident lawsuits arising from crashes in the city are filed in the Berkeley County Court of Common Pleas in Moncks Corner. Understanding the local court system matters because Berkeley County has its own judges, procedural preferences, and jury pools that can influence case strategy and outcomes.

If your case involves a federal defendant — such as a claim against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act for an accident caused by a military vehicle — it will be filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, Charleston Division. Federal cases follow different procedural rules and have no jury trial right under the FTCA, which affects both litigation strategy and settlement negotiations.

Cases involving multiple defendants across jurisdictions — for example, a crash involving both a civilian at-fault driver and a military vehicle — may require parallel proceedings in state and federal court. Navigating this procedural complexity requires an attorney familiar with both Berkeley County courts and the federal system.

Comparative Fault: South Carolina vs. Georgia

South Carolina and Georgia both use modified comparative fault systems, but the thresholds differ in a way that can determine whether you recover anything at all.

South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule under S.C. Code Section 15-38-15. You can recover damages as long as your percentage of fault is less than 51%. Your compensation is reduced by your share of fault — so if you are 30% at fault and your damages total $100,000, you would recover $70,000. But if you are found 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing.

Georgia applies a stricter threshold under O.C.G.A. Section 51-12-33. You can recover only if your fault is less than 50%. If a jury finds you exactly 50% at fault, your claim is barred entirely. This one-percentage-point difference between the two states can be outcome-determinative in close cases.

Insurance companies handling Goose Creek accident claims routinely try to inflate the injured driver's share of fault to reduce or eliminate their payout. Common tactics include blaming the victim for following too closely, failing to take evasive action, or contributing to the crash by speeding — even when the other driver's negligence was the clear primary cause. A skilled attorney knows how to counter these arguments with accident reconstruction evidence, witness testimony, and traffic camera footage that establishes the true allocation of fault.

Filing Deadlines You Cannot Afford to Miss

Every car accident claim is subject to a statute of limitations — a hard deadline after which you permanently lose the right to file suit. The applicable deadline depends on where the accident occurred and who you are suing:

  • South Carolina personal injury: 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530)
  • Georgia personal injury: 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. Section 9-3-33)
  • South Carolina wrongful death: 3 years from the date of death
  • Georgia wrongful death: 2 years from the date of death
  • Federal Tort Claims Act (military vehicle claims): Administrative claim must be filed within 2 years of the date of injury

While three years may seem like ample time, critical evidence disappears quickly. Traffic camera footage is overwritten, witness memories fade, vehicle damage is repaired or the vehicle is scrapped, and medical records become harder to connect to the accident as time passes. The strongest cases are built from evidence preserved in the days and weeks immediately following the crash, not months or years later.

How a Car Accident Lawyer Can Help

Goose Creek car accident claims involve challenges that set them apart from crashes in other areas — military traffic complications, Berkeley County court procedures, construction zone liability, and insurance companies that exploit every opportunity to minimize your claim. An experienced Charleston-area car accident lawyer can:

  • Investigate the crash scene by obtaining police reports, traffic camera footage, military police reports if applicable, and witness statements before evidence is lost
  • Identify all liable parties including at-fault drivers, trucking companies, government entities responsible for road conditions, and vehicle manufacturers
  • Document your full damages including current and future medical expenses, lost wages, diminished earning capacity, pain and suffering, and loss of quality of life
  • Handle insurance company negotiations and counter their tactics of delaying, lowballing, and shifting blame to reduce your claim
  • Navigate military-related complications including Federal Tort Claims Act procedures and claims involving active duty personnel or military vehicles
  • Prepare your case for trial in Berkeley County Court of Common Pleas or federal court, with a litigation strategy tailored to the jurisdiction

Insurance adjusters are trained to settle claims for as little as possible. They know that unrepresented claimants are more likely to accept lowball offers because they do not know the true value of their case. Having a lawyer on your side changes that dynamic entirely.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do immediately after a car accident in Goose Creek?

Call 911 and request police and EMS response. Do not move your vehicle unless it creates an immediate safety hazard. Document the scene with photographs of all vehicles, road conditions, traffic signals, and visible injuries. Exchange insurance information with the other driver but do not discuss fault or apologize. Seek medical attention within 24 hours even if you feel fine — many serious injuries, including traumatic brain injuries, do not produce symptoms immediately. Contact an attorney before giving a recorded statement to any insurance company.

How do I file a car accident claim in Berkeley County?

Your attorney will file a summons and complaint in the Berkeley County Court of Common Pleas in Moncks Corner. Before filing suit, most claims begin with an insurance demand supported by medical records, police reports, and documentation of your damages. If the insurance company refuses to offer fair compensation, litigation in Berkeley County court gives you the right to a jury trial where local jurors will evaluate your claim.

Can I recover compensation if I was partially at fault for the accident?

Yes, as long as your fault is less than 51% under South Carolina law (S.C. Code Section 15-38-15). Your recovery will be reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are found 20% at fault and your total damages are $200,000, you would recover $160,000. An attorney can help minimize the fault attributed to you by presenting evidence that supports your version of events.

What if a military vehicle caused my accident in Goose Creek?

If you are a civilian injured by a military vehicle operated by someone acting within the scope of federal duty, you may file a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act. This requires filing an administrative claim with the appropriate military branch within two years of the injury — before you can file a lawsuit. FTCA claims follow different rules than standard state court cases, and the procedural requirements are strict.

How much is my Goose Creek car accident case worth?

The value of your case depends on factors including the severity of your injuries, your medical expenses, lost income, the impact on your daily life, and the strength of the liability evidence. Cases involving traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, or wrongful death typically have significantly higher values than soft tissue injury claims. An experienced attorney can evaluate your specific circumstances and provide a realistic assessment of your claim's value.

Do I have to pay upfront to hire a car accident lawyer?

No. At Roden Law, we handle every car accident case on a contingency-fee basis, which means you pay no attorney fees unless we recover compensation for you. There are no upfront costs, no hourly bills, and no financial risk to you. We advance all case expenses and are only reimbursed if your case is successful.

If you or a loved one has been injured in a car accident in Goose Creek, on US-52, or anywhere in Berkeley County, the team at Roden Law is ready to fight for the compensation you deserve. After a car accident in South Carolina, one of the first questions injury victims ask is whether they can still recover compensation if they were partially at fault. The answer depends on South Carolina's comparative fault law -- and exactly how much fault is assigned to you. Even a small difference in fault percentage can mean the difference between a six-figure recovery and walking away with nothing.

South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault system under S.C. Code Section 15-38-15, which allows injured parties to recover damages only if their share of fault is less than 51%. If you are found 51% or more at fault for the accident, you are completely barred from recovering any compensation. Understanding how this rule applies to your Charleston accident case is critical to protecting your financial recovery.

What Is Comparative Fault in South Carolina?

Comparative fault -- sometimes called comparative negligence -- is the legal framework courts and insurance companies use to assign responsibility when more than one party contributes to an accident. Rather than treating fault as all-or-nothing, South Carolina law recognizes that multiple parties can share blame for a collision or injury.

Under S.C. Code Section 15-38-15, South Carolina uses a modified comparative fault standard. This means that an injured person's compensation is reduced in proportion to their percentage of fault. However, the law imposes a hard cutoff: if the injured person's fault reaches 51% or more, they lose the right to any recovery whatsoever.

This rule applies across all types of personal injury claims in South Carolina, including truck accidents, motorcycle crashes, slip and fall injuries, and premises liability cases.

How Modified Comparative Fault Works: The 51% Rule

The mechanics of South Carolina's modified comparative fault system are straightforward in theory but often fiercely contested in practice. Here is how it works step by step:

  1. Total damages are calculated. The jury or adjuster determines the full value of your injuries, including medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, and other losses.
  2. Fault is assigned as a percentage. Each party involved in the accident receives a percentage of fault. These percentages must add up to 100%.
  3. Your recovery is reduced by your fault percentage. Whatever percentage of fault is attributed to you, your total damages award is reduced by that same percentage.
  4. The 51% bar applies. If your assigned fault is 51% or greater, you receive nothing -- regardless of how severe your injuries are.

This threshold makes the difference between 50% and 51% fault enormously consequential. At 50% fault, you can still recover half of your damages. At 51%, you recover zero.

How Shared Fault Affects Your Dollar Recovery

To illustrate how comparative fault impacts your actual compensation, consider these examples based on a Charleston car accident with $200,000 in total damages:

Scenario 1: You Are 10% at Fault

You were driving slightly over the speed limit when another driver ran a red light and struck your vehicle. The jury assigns you 10% fault and the other driver 90% fault.

  • Total damages: $200,000
  • Your fault reduction: $200,000 x 10% = $20,000
  • Your recovery: $180,000

Scenario 2: You Are 30% at Fault

You were following too closely when the car ahead stopped suddenly without brake lights. Fault is split 30% to you and 70% to the other driver.

  • Total damages: $200,000
  • Your fault reduction: $200,000 x 30% = $60,000
  • Your recovery: $140,000

Scenario 3: You Are 50% at Fault

Both you and the other driver failed to yield at an unmarked intersection. Fault is assigned equally at 50% each.

  • Total damages: $200,000
  • Your fault reduction: $200,000 x 50% = $100,000
  • Your recovery: $100,000

Scenario 4: You Are 51% at Fault

The jury determines you bear the majority of responsibility for the crash.

  • Total damages: $200,000
  • Your recovery: $0

The jump from 50% to 51% fault eliminates your entire $200,000 claim. This is why fault allocation is one of the most heavily litigated issues in South Carolina personal injury cases.

South Carolina vs. Georgia: Comparative Fault Comparison

Roden Law represents accident victims across both South Carolina and Georgia, and the comparative fault rules differ between the two states in an important way.

For the full comparison — including how each state handles multiple defendants and what South Carolina’s 2026 statutory changes did to joint and several liability — see our guide to comparative negligence in Georgia versus South Carolina.

Factor South Carolina Georgia
Statute S.C. Code Section 15-38-15 O.C.G.A. Section 51-12-33
System Modified comparative fault Modified comparative fault
Recovery threshold Barred at 51% or more fault Barred at 50% or more fault
Equal fault (50/50) Plaintiff CAN recover Plaintiff CANNOT recover
Statute of limitations 3 years (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530) 2 years (O.C.G.A. Section 9-3-33)

The critical distinction: Georgia's threshold is stricter. In Georgia, a plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault is barred from recovery under O.C.G.A. Section 51-12-33. In South Carolina, that same plaintiff at 50% fault can still recover half of their damages. This one-percentage-point difference has significant practical implications for cases near the fault boundary.

Pure Comparative Fault vs. Modified Comparative Fault

Not every state handles shared fault the same way. Understanding the broader landscape helps explain why South Carolina's rule matters.

Pure comparative fault states (such as California and New York) allow injured parties to recover damages regardless of their fault percentage. Even a plaintiff who is 99% at fault can recover 1% of their damages. There is no threshold that bars recovery entirely.

Modified comparative fault states like South Carolina impose a cutoff point. Once the plaintiff's fault reaches or exceeds a set threshold -- 51% in South Carolina, 50% in Georgia -- recovery is completely barred. Below that threshold, damages are simply reduced in proportion to fault.

South Carolina's modified system creates high stakes around the fault determination. Insurance adjusters and defense attorneys know that pushing your fault allocation above 50% eliminates their client's liability entirely, which is why they aggressively pursue this strategy.

How Insurance Companies Use Comparative Fault Against You

Insurance companies routinely use South Carolina's comparative fault law as a tool to minimize or eliminate payouts. Common tactics include:

  • Inflating your fault percentage. An adjuster may claim you were 55% at fault when the evidence supports 30%, knowing that pushing you past the 51% threshold eliminates their obligation to pay anything.
  • Using your recorded statement against you. Adjusters ask leading questions designed to elicit admissions -- such as "Could you have stopped sooner?" or "Were you looking at your phone?" -- that they later use to argue shared fault.
  • Cherry-picking evidence. Insurers may focus on a single detail, like your speed being 3 mph over the limit, while ignoring the other driver's far more dangerous behavior such as running a stop sign.
  • Disputing medical causation. By arguing that some injuries were pre-existing, insurers reduce the total damages, which lowers the dollar amount of any recovery even before the comparative fault reduction.
  • Pressuring early settlements. Offering a quick, low settlement before you have legal representation and before the true fault allocation is established through investigation.

These strategies are especially common in pedestrian accident cases and motorcycle accident claims, where bias against the injured party often leads to inflated fault assignments.

Joint and Several Liability in South Carolina

South Carolina modified its joint and several liability rules under the South Carolina Tort Reform Act. Under current law, each defendant is generally liable only for their proportionate share of fault. This is known as several liability.

However, there are important exceptions. A defendant found to be more than 50% at fault may be held jointly and severally liable for economic damages, meaning they can be required to pay more than just their percentage share if other defendants cannot pay. This matters when multiple parties are at fault -- for example, in a truck accident involving both a negligent truck driver and a trucking company that failed to maintain the vehicle.

Understanding how fault is allocated among multiple defendants is essential because it directly affects which parties you can collect from and how much each must pay.

Common Scenarios Where Fault Is Shared

Shared fault disputes arise frequently in Charleston accident cases. Here are some of the most common situations:

Unsafe Lane Changes

One driver changes lanes without signaling, while the other driver was exceeding the speed limit. Both drivers contributed to the collision, and a jury must determine how to allocate fault between them.

Left-Turn Collisions

A driver making a left turn is struck by an oncoming vehicle that was traveling well above the speed limit. The turning driver may bear primary fault for failing to yield, but the speeding driver's excessive speed may have made the collision unavoidable. Fault might be split 60/40 or 70/30 depending on the specifics.

Pedestrian Crossings

A pedestrian crossing outside a crosswalk is struck by a driver who was texting. The pedestrian's jaywalking and the driver's distraction both contributed to the accident. In Charleston, these disputes often arise near King Street, Meeting Street, and other high-traffic downtown corridors.

Rear-End Collisions With Contributing Factors

While the trailing driver is generally presumed at fault in rear-end collisions, comparative fault may apply if the lead vehicle had non-functioning brake lights, made a sudden stop without reason, or was illegally double-parked.

Premises Liability With Visitor Negligence

A customer slips on a wet floor in a Charleston retail store. The store failed to place warning signs, but the customer was looking at their phone and missed a verbal warning from an employee. Both parties share some degree of responsibility.

How a Charleston Accident Lawyer Fights Comparative Fault Arguments

When insurance companies or defense attorneys try to shift blame onto you, an experienced Charleston personal injury lawyer uses several strategies to protect your recovery:

  • Accident reconstruction. Expert analysis of skid marks, vehicle damage patterns, road conditions, and traffic signal timing can establish exactly what happened and contradict inflated fault claims.
  • Surveillance and dashcam footage. Video evidence from traffic cameras, nearby businesses, or vehicle dashcams often tells a clearer story than competing witness accounts.
  • Police report analysis. While police reports are not conclusive on fault, citations issued at the scene -- such as failure to yield or running a red light -- carry significant weight in fault allocation.
  • Cell phone records. If the at-fault driver was texting or on a call at the time of the crash, phone records can prove distraction and shift fault away from you.
  • Expert medical testimony. Medical experts can refute claims that your injuries were pre-existing, ensuring your full damages are calculated before any comparative fault reduction.
  • Witness depositions. Sworn testimony from eyewitnesses, taken under oath before trial, can lock in favorable accounts of the accident before memories fade or stories change.

The goal is always to minimize your assigned fault percentage -- because every percentage point directly affects your dollar recovery. Reducing your fault from 35% to 20% on a $300,000 case means an additional $45,000 in your pocket.

South Carolina Filing Deadlines

South Carolina gives accident victims three years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code Section 15-3-530. While three years may seem like ample time, comparative fault cases often require extensive investigation, expert analysis, and evidence preservation that should begin immediately.

Key reasons not to delay:

  • Surveillance footage is typically overwritten within 30 to 90 days.
  • Witness memories fade and become less reliable over time.
  • Physical evidence at the accident scene degrades or is removed.
  • Insurance companies may begin building their comparative fault argument while you wait.

If your accident occurred in Georgia, the deadline is even shorter -- just two years under O.C.G.A. Section 9-3-33. Missing the filing deadline in either state permanently bars your claim regardless of fault allocation.

Protect Your Recovery After a Charleston Accident

South Carolina's comparative fault rule means that your percentage of fault directly determines your compensation -- and crossing the 51% threshold eliminates it entirely. Insurance companies know this and will aggressively try to shift blame onto you. Having an experienced attorney who understands how to investigate fault, counter inflated blame arguments, and present your case effectively is essential to protecting your financial recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What is comparative fault in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: SC follows a modified comparative fault rule (S.C. Code section 15-38-15). You can recover damages if your fault is less than 51 percent. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20 percent at fault and damages are 100,000 dollars, you recover 80,000 dollars.

_roden_faqs.question: How is SC comparative fault different from Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia bars recovery if you are 50 percent or more at fault (O.C.G.A. section 51-12-33). SC bars recovery at 51 percent or more. This one percent difference matters in close cases.

_roden_faqs.question: How do insurance companies use comparative fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurers routinely argue the injured person was partially at fault to reduce the payout. Common arguments include following too closely, distracted driving, not wearing a seatbelt, or crossing outside a crosswalk.

_roden_faqs.question: Does wearing a seatbelt affect my claim in SC?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Under S.C. Code § 56-5-6540(C), a seatbelt violation is not negligence per se or contributory negligence and is not admissible as evidence in a civil action. South Carolina does not reduce your recovery by any set percentage for seatbelt non-use, and an insurer cannot put that evidence before a jury. If an adjuster raises it, that is not a basis South Carolina law recognizes.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault determined?
_roden_faqs.answer: Fault is determined by the jury based on evidence including police reports, witness testimony, traffic camera footage, accident reconstruction, and expert opinions.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if I was mostly at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: In SC, yes, as long as your fault is less than 51 percent. In GA, you must be less than 50 percent at fault. Even at 49 percent fault in SC, you would recover 51 percent of your damages.
